column4: Replace blanks with an explicit 'Unknown' category (do not guess a profile). Flag the clients so advisors can collect the missing questionnaire.
column5: Risk profile drives suitability decisions. Imputing it from age or tier would invent regulatory-relevant data.
column6: Medium: 'Unknown' clients drop out of risk-based analysis until the data is collected.

column3: 20 client_ids appear twice (20 extra rows), which breaks the primary key. e.g. '171', '195', '252', '322'.
column4: For each duplicated id, keep the row whose last_name is valid (letters only) and drop the corrupted copy; if both are valid, keep the first occurrence.
column5: A dimension table needs one row per key, or joins to the fact tables double-count fees, transactions and AUM.
column6: Low: the copies are identical except for the garbled last name, so no real information is lost.

column3: 20 of the duplicated ids are the same client re-loaded with a corrupted last name (near-duplicate records).
column4: Resolve by deduplicating on client_id (see above) rather than on the full row, because a full-row check misses these.
column5: An exact-duplicate check reports 0 duplicates here, so the problem would slip through without a key-based check.
column6: Low: the matching columns confirm the rows are the same person.

column3: 20 values contain digits or symbols (e.g. 'N3Lson', 'G@Rcia', 'H@Rding', 'P3Rez'), e.g. '3' for 'e', '0' for 'o', '@' for 'a', '!' for 'i'.
column4: Where the client_id has a clean duplicate, use the clean name. Otherwise map 3->e, 0->o, @->a, !->i, then title-case.
column5: The substitutions follow a consistent character-swap pattern and the clean copies confirm the intended spelling.
column6: Low: the fixes are verified against the clean copies; any name without a clean copy should be reviewed by hand.

column3: 5 values are impossible for an investment client (< 18 or > 110): '0', '999', '-5'. They look like placeholder or sentinel values.
column4: Set these ages to null (NaN) and keep the column as an integer type. Do not replace them with the mean or median.
column5: 0, -5 and 999 are data-entry defaults, not real ages. Imputing a value would hide the error and bias age-band analysis.
column6: Low: very few rows are affected; they are excluded only from age-based analysis.

column3: Inconsistent format: 202 rows use full state names (e.g. 'Florida', 'Pennsylvania', 'Delaware', 'Ohio') while the rest use two-letter codes. This gives 40 distinct values for 20 real states.
column4: Map full names to their USPS two-letter code with a lookup dictionary and store every value in upper case.
column5: Grouping by state would otherwise split 'PA' and 'Pennsylvania' into separate states and undercount each.
column6: Very low: a name-to-code mapping is deterministic.

column3: 50 values have leading/trailing spaces and 50 are in ALL CAPS (e.g. '  EAST MARK  ', '  SOUTH KIMBERLYSTAD  ', '  ROSALESSHIRE  '), while the rest are in title case.
column4: Trim whitespace with str.strip(), then apply str.title().
column5: '  EAST MARK  ' and 'East Mark' are the same city but would be counted separately in grouping and joins.
column6: Very low: title-casing may change a few spellings (e.g. 'McAllen' -> 'Mcallen'), which is acceptable here.

column3: 234 ZIP codes have fewer than 5 digits (e.g. '3897', '3946', '9118', '7206'). Leading zeros were dropped when the column was stored as a number.
column4: Keep zip_code as text and left-pad to 5 digits with str.zfill(5) (e.g. 3897 -> 03897).
column5: ZIP codes are identifiers, not quantities. Northeast ZIPs (NJ, MA, CT...) start with 0.
column6: Low: padding restores the original value; note that the ZIPs do not always match the state in this synthetic data.

column3: 524 rows hold the value '529' (a college-savings plan), which tools like Excel or pandas can read as the number 529.
column4: Always read the column as text (dtype=str). Optionally relabel as '529 Plan' for clarity.
column5: If the column is converted to a number, the category turns into an integer or makes the whole column mixed-type.
column6: Very low: relabelling is cosmetic; the value itself is valid.

column3: 233 values are statistical outliers (> Q3 + 3*IQR, max 49,901,583.57). All of them belong to UHNW clients and match their tier.

column5: The large values are real ultra-high-net-worth balances, not errors. Removing them would delete the most valuable clients.
column6: Low: the only risk is skewed averages if the mean is used.

column3: Mixed date formats: 2469 rows are YYYY-MM-DD and 76 are MM/DD/YYYY (e.g. '01/02/2016', '10/26/2016', '08/21/2020'). The column is stored as text, not as a date.
column4: Parse each format explicitly (format='%Y-%m-%d', then format='%m/%d/%Y' for the rest) and convert to a single datetime column stored as ISO YYYY-MM-DD.
column5: 43 of the slash dates have a day > 12, which proves the order is month/day, not day/month. Mixed text dates cannot be sorted or used for tenure calculations.
column6: Low: slash dates with day <= 12 are assumed to be MM/DD like the rest; an explicit format prevents mis-parsing.

column4: Map True/yes/1/Y -> True and False/no/0/N -> False; store as a boolean column. Null anything else.
